strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem with a simple, modular idea: repair misaligned patches along an existing seam, then recompute locally constrained seams. This could improve existing pipelines without retraining.

Table I reports consistent improvements across four seam-cutting methods and 79 image pairs from three datasets. For example, on SEAGULL, Baseline+LPAM increases seam SSIM from 0.638 to 0.696 and PSNR from 26.20 to 28.31. Figures 1, 5, and 6 also demonstrate visible structural improvements.

The design explicitly considers compatibility with the existing mosaic through flow modification and preservation of boundary labels during local graph cuts. Figure 3 usefully illustrates why unrestricted local warping can introduce artifacts.

The pipeline is clearly motivated, includes pseudocode and several parameter settings, cites its underlying methods and benchmark datasets, and provides a code/dataset link. The concrete failure examples and explanations in Section IV-D help establish the intended operating conditions.
weaknesses: The contribution is insufficiently distinguished from closely related approaches. SEAGULL [25] already uses seam-guided local alignment, and the cited method [21] couples dense matching, seam estimation, and warping. Quantitative comparisons only add LPAM to seam cutters using the same REW initialization; Figure 6 provides just one qualitative comparison with Parallax and SEAGULL. These results demonstrate useful augmentation but do not adequately establish its advantage over existing alignment-and-seam strategies.

The central deformation operation is ambiguous. Equation (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Equation (5) and the accompanying explanation define a scalar sigmoid of normalized pixel position. The manuscript should explicitly specify how this positional weight modifies the flow. The sigmoid alone also does not establish the claimed consistency at patch boundaries. These appear potentially correctable, but currently impede faithful reproduction of the main operation.

There are no dataset-level ablations establishing the value of error-based patch selection, sigmoid flow modification, or boundary constraints. Figure 3 offers only a single qualitative comparison of sigmoid settings. Comparisons against simpler local corrections and sensitivity to patch extent and the stopping threshold would clarify which design choices produce the gains.

The quantitative metrics measure agreement between patches around the seam, rather than independently assessing final mosaic fidelity. SSIM also drives repair selection. These measurements cannot establish whether improved correspondence comes at the cost of geometric distortion or artifacts elsewhere. The acknowledged failures are relevant: uniformly poor seams can pass the relative-error stopping rule, and small-patch repairs can introduce discontinuities. Their frequency and per-image regressions are not reported.

The efficiency claim is only partially supported. Table III reports approximately 7–10 seconds of additional LPAM processing, exceeding several underlying seam-cutting runtimes. Image resolutions, scaling behavior, and runtime comparisons with alternative seam-guided alignment methods are missing, so the claimed computational advantage remains unclear.
